title: Configure Activity - ART Mechanistic Model
desc: No control measures in close proximity of the source.
Wetting systems that wet the process at the point of release (focusing on the emission source) to agglomerate and bind the fine particles to prevent dust from being dispersed into the workroom air.
Post generation suppression of airborne contaminants to reduce dust levels. Knockdown of a contaminant after it has been emitted.

Physical containment or enclosure of the source of emission. The air within the enclosure is not actively ventilated or extracted. The enclosure is not opened during the activity. This class reflects “add on” enclosures and does not include inherently closed systems (like pipelines)

Physical containment or enclosure of the source of emission. The air within the enclosure is not actively ventilated or extracted. The enclosure is not opened during the activity.

The process is contained with a loose lid or cover, which is not air tight. This includes tapping molten metal through covered launders and placing a loose lid on a ladle.

This class also includes bags or liners fitted around transfer points from source to receiving vessel. These include Muller seals, Stott head and single bag, and associated clamps and closures.

Physical containment or enclosure of the source of emission. The air within the enclosure is not actively ventilated or extracted. The enclosure is not opened during the activity.

The material transfer is enclosed with the receiving vessel being docked or sealed to the source vessel.

Examples include sealing heads, transfer containers and multiple o-rings. Inflatable packing head with continuous liner ensures a seal is maintained during the powder transfer and the continuous plastic liner prevents direct contact with the product. The correct type of tie off must be used.

Physical containment or enclosure of the source of emission. The air within the enclosure is not actively ventilated or extracted. The enclosure is not opened during the activity.

The substance is contained within a sealed and enclosed system. This class includes metal smelting furnaces or atomisation units.

The material transfer is entirely enclosed with high containment valves (e.g. split butterfly valves and direct couplings, which consist of two sections which connect together to allow the opening of the valve). At the end of the material transfer the two halves are separated, forming a seal on both the process equipment and the material container. The system is designed to minimise the surface area which can contact the material or pairs of valves with wash space between them.
A canopy hood placed over a hot process to receive the plume of contaminant-laden air given off. For cold processes with no thermal uplift, canopy hoods are ineffective (HSE, 2008).

A receiving hood can be applied wherever a process produces a contaminant cloud with a strong and predictable direction (e.g. a grinding wheel). The contaminant cloud is propelled into the hood by process-induced air movement. The face of the hood must be big enough to receive the contaminant cloud and the extraction empties the hood of contaminated air at least as fast as it is filled.

Fixed capturing hoods located in close proximity of and directed at the source of emission. The design is such that the work is performed in the capture zone of the ventilation system and the capture is indicated at the workplace.

Movable LEV systems such as hoods with extendable arms. The design of the system does not prevent work being performed outside the capture zone of the system and worker behaviour can influence the effectiveness of the system.
LEV systems integrated in a process or equipment that cannot be separated from the primary emission source.

In a horizontal laminar flow booth, contaminated air is extracted through holes situated at the rear of the booth which creates a horizontal laminar air flow. The air is filtered prior to being discharged to the atmosphere. The booth contains the source and has maximally one side open.

In a downward laminar flow booth, a curtain of descending laminar air flow is created between the ceiling and the rear of the booth where exhaust grills are located in the lower section. The booth contains the source and has maximally one side open.

Spray rooms and laminar down-flow booths (with the size of a room which contains both the source and the worker) are not considered to be a localised control and will be treated together with the dispersion questions at a later stage.

Any form of permanent encapsulation or encasing of the source of which maximally one side is open with a well designed local exhaust ventilation system (e.g. laminar air flow). The design of both the enclosure and the ventilation system is such that the influence of worker behaviour is minimal (e.g. an alarm system prevents the worker from using the fume cupboard in case the system is not working properly).
Any form of permanent encapsulation or encasing of the source of which maximally the front side is open with a proper local exhaust ventilation system.

In case the type of local exhaust ventilation system is unknown or not specified, this default LEV category can be selected. Note that this default category results in a low reduction of the estimated personal exposure level. An attempt should be made to more specifically define the type of local exhaust ventilation.

Large plastic bags, available in different design and sizes are fitted with gloves which allow products to be handled in a contained way.

An adaptor piece is necessary between the glove bag and the process equipment.

The glove bag must be designed specifically for the task and the quantity of material to be handled.

Various other items such as pass-out boxes, inlet filters, and drains are added to meet specific needs.

Note: use of glove bags does not negate the need to implement a long term permanent technological solution.
Large plastic bags, available in different design and sizes are fitted with gloves which allow products to be handled in a contained way without exhaust ventilation.

Large plastic bags, available in different design and sizes are fitted with gloves which allow products to be handled in a contained way. The glove bag is maintained with filtration and ventilation at specific flow rates.

Any form of permanent encapsulation or encasing of the source (which are not opened during the given activity) with a well designed local exhaust ventilation system.

The design of both the enclosure and the ventilation system is such that the influence of worker behaviour is minimal (e.g. the enclosure cannot be opened before the substance is properly vented).

A low specification glove box is specified as:
  • Single chamber, simple access doors or pass box
  • Not safe change glove
  • Single HEPA filtered extract air
  • Not safe change filters
  • Manual cleaning

A medium specification glove box is specified as:
  • Two or more chambers if large area bin docking or high dust levels expected
  • Safe change or push through filters are required
  • Solid (stainless steel) construction for durability
  • Size is dependent on the task to be carried out
  • Safe change filters are required
  • Air should be single or double HEPA filtered and or exhausted directly to the atmosphere after single HEPA filtration.
  • The equipment should be maintained under negative pressure and the air flow and filter condition continuously monitored.
  • Emergency air extraction should start up automatically in the event of a leak or a damaged glove.
  • Interlocked air locks should be used to prevent high dust concentrations in the area of the transfer ports and reduce risk. (escape of the contaminant during transfer of materials into and out of the glove box).
  • Glove changes should be able to be carried out without breaking containment
  • Waste disposal ports are required. Correct sealing of continuous liners.
  • Manual cleaning

A high specification glove box is specified as:
  • Two or more chambers
  • Safe change filters are required
  • Stainless steel construction
  • Size is dependent on the task to be carried out
  • Safe change filters are required
  • Air should be single or double HEPA filtered and or exhausted directly to the atmosphere after single HEPA filtration.
  • The equipment should be maintained under negative pressure and the air flow and filter condition continuously monitored.
  • Emergency air extraction should start up automatically in the event of a leak or a damaged glove.
  • Interlocked air locks should be used to prevent the escape of the contaminant during transfer of materials into and out of the glove box.
  • Glove changes should be able to be carried out without breaking containment
  • Waste disposal ports are required.
  • Integrated sampling and contained drum charging
  • Sealed and high containment transfer ports (contained transfer couplings, rapid transfer ports (RTPs), alpha/beta valves etc.)
  • Including waste removal and change parts
  • Wash in place
  • Alarmed

Reduction of vapour emission during storage, loading and off-loading of gasoline or other liquids, and during re-fuelling of a vehicle, by the combination of a vapour collection system and a vapour control unit. Vapour collection is a passive process where the volume of liquid transferred is equal to the volume of vapour transported back to the tank. The system only works properly when no other escape openings are present.

title: Configure Activity - ART Mechanistic Model
text: Specify the segregation for this emission source then click Next.

Segregation of the source is defined as isolation of sources from the work environment in a separate room without direct containment of the source itself. The segregated area is not entered by the worker during a given activity or working shift.
desc: The source is not isolated from the work environment.

Sources are partially segregated from the work environment by isolating the source in a separate room (e.g. with open doors and/or windows to the adjacent area). This segregated area is generally not entered by the worker during a given activity or working shift. The air within the separate room is not actively ventilated.

Sources are partially segregated from the work environment by isolating the source in a separate room (with open doors and/or windows). This segregated area is generally not entered by the worker during a given activity or working shift. The air within the separate area is actively ventilated and the recirculated air is filtered or there is no air recirculation.

Sources are completely segregated from the work environment by isolating the source in a fully enclosed and separate room (incl. closed doors & windows). This segregated area is generally not entered by the worker during a given activity or working shift. The air within the separate area is not ventilated.

Sources are completely segregated from the work environment by isolating the source in a fully enclosed and separate room (incl. closed doors & windows). The air within the separate area is actively ventilated and the recirculated air is filtered or there is no air recirculation. The segregated area is generally not entered by the worker during a given activity or working shift.
validation: Select the segregation for this emission source.

title: Configure Activity - ART Mechanistic Model
text: Select the personal enclosure available to the worker then click Next to continue.
desc: No personal enclosure within a work environment.

Partial personal enclosure is a partially open cabin or room (e.g. open windows, door) where a worker is partially protected but still in direct contact with the work environment. The air within the personal enclosure is not actively ventilated.

Partial personal enclosure is a partially open cabin or room (e.g. open windows, door) where a worker is partially protected but still in direct contact with the work environment. The air within the personal enclosure is ventilated and a positive pressure is maintained inside the personal enclosure.
Worker resides inside an enclosed cabin or room (door & windows closed) for the entire duration of the activity. The air within the separate room is not actively ventilated.

Worker resides inside an enclosed cabin or room (door and/or windows closed) for the entire duration of the activity. The air within the personal enclosure is actively ventilated and filtered and a positive pressure is maintained inside the personal enclosure.

title: Configure Activity - ART Mechanistic Model
desc: Both the source and the worker are located indoors. The indoor environment should be enclosed by walls on each side and a roof on top. A garage with the garage door open should be treated as an indoor environment.

Both the source and the worker are located outdoors. It is assumed there are two situations outdoors where the scenario may be located: close to buildings or away from buildings or other obstructions.

The spray room is defined as: a fully enclosed room between 30 and 1000 m³ with at least 10 air changes per hour. The spray room needs to be regularly checked and maintained. The workers in the spray room need to be properly trained in correctly using the room (e.g. wearing air-fed breathing equipment, knowing the clearance time of the room, good positioning of the worker relative to the source and the ventilation). The spray room needs to run under negative pressure (so any air leakage is inward).

The spray room must meet the following conditions:
  • The spray room is a fully enclosed, unidirectional spray room of volume between 30 and 1000 m³ with at least 10 air changes per hour.
  • The spray room has been designed by a competent ventilation engineer, the airflow performance is regularly checked and the ventilation system is maintained.
  • The spray room needs to run under negative pressure (i.e. so any air leakage is inward).
  • The workers in the spray room must be properly trained in correctly using the room (e.g. operation of the ventilation system, good positioning of the worker relative to the source and the ventilation, knowing the ventilation clearance time of the room).

The spray room must meet the following conditions:
  • The spray room is a fully enclosed, unidirectional downflow spray room of volume between 30 and 1000 m³ with at least 10 air changes per hour
  • The spray room has been designed by a competent ventilation engineer, the airflow performance is regularly checked and the ventilation system is maintained
  • The spray room needs to run under negative pressure (i.e. so any air leakage is inward)
  • The workers in the spray room must be properly trained in correctly using the room (e.g. operation of the ventilation system, good positioning of the worker relative to the source and the ventilation, knowing the ventilation clearance time of the room)

A curtain of descending laminar air is created between the ceiling and the rear of the booth where exhaust grilles are located at the lower section. The worker must not stand at the exhaust grilles and standing in-between the source and the grilles will reduce the effectiveness of the booth. The exhaust volume is typically between 3500-4000 m³/h (per 1m width).
  • The booths must completely enclose the work task and the worker.
  • Booth sizes are adaptable to the work task and process equipment and can have varying levels of filtration.
  • The filter should have high dust holding capacity, and performance and volume air flow need to be checked regularly.
  • For booth down flow and laminar flow booths capture velocity approx 0.5 m/second.
  • A safe work line (SWL) marks the limit of effective containment and dust capture.
  • Flow booths can be equipped with partial or full screens with glove ports, potentially offering a further level of containment.
Partial screens covering the majority of the front of the process/booth; however there may be relatively small openings for operator hands and/or gaps at the top and bottom of the booth.

Partial screen covering the majority of front of process/booth and is fitted with glove ports to allow the operator handle the product; however there may be relatively small gaps at the top and/or bottom of the booth.
Full screen covering the entire front of the process/booth and is fitted with glove ports.

text: ART offers two types of exposure prediction:

ART calculates an overall distribution for full-shift exposures. In this case, the 90th percentile provides the exposure level, which has a 10% probability of being exceeded by the exposure from a randomly selected worker on a randomly selected day.

This measure can also be used for short-term estimates, but it should be recognised that short-term exposures (less than 60 minutes) may have a different pattern of variability. The ART full-shift measure is based on variability estimates derived from measurements collected over periods of four hours or longer.

ART calculates the distribution of workers' long-term average (mean) exposure (e.g. over a period of months). In this case, the 90th percentile provides the long-term mean exposure level, which has a 10% probability of being exceeded by the long-term exposure from a randomly selected worker.

From a scientific perspective, the distribution of long-term average exposure is the most appropriate one when considering chronic health end points, or when comparing exposure levels with chronic toxicity data.
For each type of exposure ART supports a range of percentiles (50th, 75th, 90th, 95th and 99th) and confidence intervals (50%, 80%, 90% and 95%).

ART calculates percentiles and confidence intervals using mathematical simulation techniques. Although a large number of iterations are performed, occasionally very small differences in output can occur between model runs.

ART 1.5 provides an extensive library of different exposure measurement datasets to choose from. Each dataset has an accompanying concise description of the exposure scenario to assist users in selecting exposure measurements analogous to their scenario. Exposure data are grouped together based on the activity classes (task categories) and the product used. As a general rule, exposure data from a given field study with the same activity (e.g. spraying of liquids) and product (e.g. antifouling paints) are grouped together into one scenario. A given study might be grouped into separate scenarios (e.g. spraying with and without LEV) if distinct differences in exposure determinants or controls are applicable and provided that the dataset consisted of a sufficient number of measurements. In some instances, a scenario is described by multiple activities (and same product exposure) with a presumed high exposure potential during a given exposure period (e.g. spraying, brushing and sweeping during a full shift).

The measurements included in the ART Exposure Data Library (EDL) were all included in the calibration of the mechanistic model of ART and complied with the data quality criteria used in this exercise (namely, that core information on sampling and analytical methods was documented and all the ART modifying factors be assessed or reliably assumed for all activities during the measurement period). From the calibration exercise only studies with five or more measurements were retained for inclusion in the EDL.

An important feature of ART is the continual updating of the exposure model. Additional exposure data will be added in the future to ensure that exposure estimates are based on the most recent and up-to-date exposure data available.
How potentially analogous measurement data are identified in ART v1.5
ART v1.5 identifies potentially analogous measurement data by searching the ART EDL on exposure form and activity class. The search returns all datasets relating to the same

, or in the case of composite scenarios with multiple activities, all data sets relating to the same exposure form with at least one activity in common with the user's scenario. The exposure form depends upon the product type, and for liquids, the vapour pressure at the process temperature.

As implemented in ART v1.5 the Bayesian model only supports the use of fully analogous exposure measurements, that is, measurements that are supposed to relate to essentially the same exposure scenario that ART is being used to assess. The search algorithms implemented in ART v1.5 identify all potentially analogous measurement series in the ART exposure library. Users are required to make their own expert judgement as to which, if any, of the datasets are appropriate for assessing exposures for their scenario, mindful that with fully analogous datasets ART v1.5 does not consider any additional scenario-to-scenario extrapolation uncertainty. ART v1.5.
The measurements should relate to the same activity; any supplementary determinants e.g. orientation for spray activities, drop height, should be comparable.

For scenarios relating to exposures to vapours, data should relate to the same substance and share a similar process temperature, and if not a pure substance, the substance concentrations should be broadly the same and the mixtures should have similar activation factors. For non-volatile liquids (mists) and dusts the concentration of the substance need not match that of the user's scenario as a concentration adjustment is made in the Bayesian update (see next section). Hence there are no specific substance related requirements for non-volatile liquids other than that they substances (or mixtures) should have similar viscosity. For dusts, measurements should only be considered fully analogous if they relate to substances with similar dustiness scores as the user's scenario (i.e. the same dustiness category) with similar moisture levels.
ART assumes that dispersion of an airborne substance is related to levels of ventilation and (if indoor) room volumes. Both these factors should be comparable to the user's scenario.
Separation and segregation of the workers and sources should be comparable to the conditions pertaining to the user's scenario; local controls should be of the same type.

Measurements in the EDL generally relate to a monitored period of exposure generating activity rather than being time-weighted average exposures for a whole shift. As ART predicts time-weighted average exposures it is important that users do not specify a period of non-exposure and then perform a Bayesian update with measurements that relate only to the exposure generating activity. Beyond this the duration of measurement need not be comparable to the user's scenario, though it is important to recognise that ART is not configured to predict short-term exposures (less than fifteen minutes) and measurements with sampling times shorter than this are likely to exhibit greater variability.

A short description of each measurement dataset provides details of each of these exposure-modifying factors and is available from the ART search results. In many instances these descriptions should provide sufficient detail with which to assess the suitability of a dataset, however where users require further detail and the data are in the public domain, users should refer to the referenced reports or journal articles.
Concentration adjustments to exposure measurements used in a Bayesian update

An underlying assumption made in ART, similar to those made in exposure assessments for biocides and plant protection products, is that for dusts and non-volatile liquids (mists) exposure to a substance can be derived from a measured or modelled exposure to the dust or mist under the assumption that exposures to the substance will be proportional to the substance concentration in the dust or liquid.

As ART predicts exposure to the substance and not the total dust or mist (except where a pure substance is being used) the Bayesian update makes the following concentration adjustment: each measured value is multiplied by the ratio of the substance concentration provided by the user and the substance concentration for that measurement. For example, if the user has specified a substance concentration of 2% and the substance concentrations for the measurements were 1%, then ART will double all the measured exposures before using them to update the mechanistic model predictions.

In more complex situations where users have defined multiple exposure sources with differing substance concentrations, ART bases the concentration adjustment upon the source that, as predicted by the mechanistic model, makes the greatest contribution to the time-weighted exposure.
Concentration adjustments for dusts and mists are also applied to users own exposure data

Analogous data are uploaded to ART in the form of CSV. The CSV file must contain the following columns:
An identifier for the dataset, as a string.
An identifier for the site, as a string.
An identifier for the worker, as a string.
The value of exposure in mg/m
, as a floating point number ('with a '.' or ',' as the decimal place according to your computer settings).
The concentration of the active substance in the measured formulation (if applicable), as a floating point number between 0 and 1 (i.e. 0–100%). If left blank, no concentration correction is made.

Whether or not the exposure was below the limit of detection. The values TRUE, 1, T and < (case insensitive) are recognised as true. The values FALSE, 0, F or an empty string, (also case insensitive) are recognised as false. Any other value will cause an error.
The ratio of exposures for the dataset, as a positive floating point number. Blank values are allowed, but the column must be present.

desc: Both the source and the worker are located indoors. The indoor environment should be enclosed by walls on each side and a roof on top. A garage with the garage door open should be treated as an indoor environment.

Both the source and the worker are located outdoors. It is assumed there are two situations outdoors where the scenario may be located: close to buildings or away from buildings or other obstructions.

The spray room is defined as: a fully enclosed room between 30 and 1000 m³ with at least 10 air changes per hour. The spray room needs to be regularly checked and maintained. The workers in the spray room need to be properly trained in correctly using the room (e.g. wearing air-fed breathing equipment, knowing the clearance time of the room, good positioning of the worker relative to the source and the ventilation). The spray room needs to run under negative pressure (so any air leakage is inward).

The spray room must meet the following conditions:
  • The spray room is a fully enclosed, unidirectional spray room of volume between 30 and 1000 m³ with at least 10 air changes per hour.
  • The spray room has been designed by a competent ventilation engineer, the airflow performance is regularly checked and the ventilation system is maintained.
  • The spray room needs to run under negative pressure (i.e. so any air leakage is inward).
  • The workers in the spray room must be properly trained in correctly using the room (e.g. operation of the ventilation system, good positioning of the worker relative to the source and the ventilation, knowing the ventilation clearance time of the room).

The spray room must meet the following conditions:
  • The spray room is a fully enclosed, unidirectional downflow spray room of volume between 30 and 1000 m³ with at least 10 air changes per hour
  • The spray room has been designed by a competent ventilation engineer, the airflow performance is regularly checked and the ventilation system is maintained
  • The spray room needs to run under negative pressure (i.e. so any air leakage is inward)
  • The workers in the spray room must be properly trained in correctly using the room (e.g. operation of the ventilation system, good positioning of the worker relative to the source and the ventilation, knowing the ventilation clearance time of the room)

A curtain of descending laminar air is created between the ceiling and the rear of the booth where exhaust grilles are located at the lower section. The worker must not stand at the exhaust grilles and standing in-between the source and the grilles will reduce the effectiveness of the booth. The exhaust volume is typically between 3500-4000 m³/h (per 1m width).
  • The booths must completely enclose the work task and the worker.
  • Booth sizes are adaptable to the work task and process equipment and can have varying levels of filtration.
  • The filter should have high dust holding capacity, and performance and volume air flow need to be checked regularly.
  • For booth down flow and laminar flow booths capture velocity approx 0.5 m/second.
  • A safe work line (SWL) marks the limit of effective containment and dust capture.
  • Flow booths can be equipped with partial or full screens with glove ports, potentially offering a further level of containment.
Partial screens covering the majority of the front of the process/booth; however there may be relatively small openings for operator hands and/or gaps at the top and bottom of the booth.

Partial screen covering the majority of front of process/booth and is fitted with glove ports to allow the operator handle the product; however there may be relatively small gaps at the top and/or bottom of the booth.
Full screen covering the entire front of the process/booth and is fitted with glove ports.
